Description Ecological - general:
Tidally influenced coastal forest ecosystems dominated by halophytic woody species adapted to saline conditions and regular inundation.
Mangroves comprise specialised salt-tolerant tree and shrub communities occurring in tropical and subtropical intertidal zones, characterised by pneumatophores, prop roots, and vivipary. In India, they range from the extensive Sundarbans (dominated by Heritiera and Excoecaria) in the east to smaller patches along the western coast (dominated by Avicennia and Rhizophora), with structural complexity varying from tall closed canopies to stunted shrubby formations based on salinity and tidal amplitude. These ecosystems show minimal seasonal variation in canopy cover but may exhibit phenological changes in flowering and fruiting.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB  (4-3-2) composites, mangroves appear dark green to brownish-green.
-  in NIR-R-G (543), they show bright red to crimson due to high chlorophyll content and moisture.
- In SWIR-NIR-R, they appear bright green as strong reflectance is seen in the NIR channel.  
- Seasonal variations are subtle with slightly darker tones during monsoon months due to increased moisture and sediment load in surrounding waters  whilst tidal variations can affect spectral signatures based on water levels during image acquisition.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Medium to coarse
- Shape: Varrying
- Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general: Forests maintaining green foliage throughout the year with less than 25% deciduous species, typically occurring in areas receiving over 2000mm annual rainfall or in temperature-limited high elevation zones. These forests encompass tropical wet evergreens of the Western Ghats and North-East (dominated by Dipterocarpus, Mesua, Hopea), semi-evergreens with 25-75% evergreen species, montane temperate forests (including Quercus, Rhododendron), and coniferous formations (Pinus, Cedrus, Abies) of the Himalayas. They exhibit multi-layered canopy structure with emergents reaching 45-60m in tropical zones, dense understory vegetation including bamboo patches, and high epiphytic loads in humid regions. Whilst maintaining year-round green cover, these forests show subtle phenological patterns in leaf flush, flowering, and fruiting cycles.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, evergreen forests appear deep green to dark green throughout the year
- in NIR-R-G, they show consistent bright red to deep red signatures indicating high photosynthetic activity.
- In SWIR-NIR-R, they display bright green tones and these tones are similar between the Dry and the overall season; there is hardly any change in tone (compared to decidious forest). 
- Seasonal variations are minimal
- In comparison to deciduous forest, the NDVI behaves more stably across the seasons.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Course/rough
- Shape: Varying
- Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general: Forests where more than 75% of canopy trees shed leaves during the dry season, typically occurring in areas with 600-2000mm rainfall and a pronounced dry period of 3-6 months. These include moist deciduous forests dominated by Tectona grandis and Shorea robusta in areas with 1200-2000mm rainfall, dry deciduous forests with Anogeissus and Terminalia species in 600-1200mm zones, and thorn forests transitioning to savanna woodlands in areas below 600mm. They exhibit distinct seasonal rhythms with synchronous leaf fall during dry months (December-May), varying from complete deciduousness in dry zones to partial leaf retention in moister areas, and understory bamboo (Dendrocalamus, Bambusa) that may remain green. Regional patterns include sal forests in central and eastern India showing earlier leaf fall than teak forests of peninsular India.
Description FCC - general:
-  For the bands 543 (NIR-R-G) - bright red during the growing season, dropping to dull brown/grey when leafless.
- In comparison to evergreen, the red tones are more brighter and/or brown red tinged red. 
- For the bands 6-5-4 (SWIR-NIR-R) and 6-5-4Dry there is a difference in colour for decidious versus evergreen forest with dry season defined as the lower 25% percentile of the NDVI. 
- In comparison to evergreen forest, seasonal amplitude in vegetation indices (NDVI varying from 0.2-0.8) is diagnostic for deciduous forests, with peak greenness in September-October and minimum in March-April, varying by latitude and elevation. This can also be seen from the scripts especially the updated version of the Step_02_Collect_and_Export_Samples.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Medium to coarse
-  Shape: Varrying 
- Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general: Forest areas not clearly classifiable into specific evergreen or deciduous categories, including mixed composition forests, degraded forests, secondary growth, and successional stages. This category encompasses forests with mixed evergreen-deciduous composition (25-75% of either type), secondary forests regenerating after disturbance, degraded forest patches with altered structure and composition, and forest edges showing ecotonal characteristics. These areas often display irregular canopy structure, pioneer species mixed with climax species, variable phenology depending on species mix, and may include exotic plantations reverting to natural forest. They represent transitional states between forest types or successional stages that don't fit neat classification categories.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB (4-3-2), mixed forests show intermediate green tones with a patchy appearance.
- In NIR-R-G (5-4-3), they display variable red signatures with spatial heterogeneity reflecting species mix.
- SWIR-NIR-R (6-5-4), they show mottled patterns of bright green tones to pink (degraded forest) based on moisture and leaf characteristics.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Medium to coarse
-  Shape: Varrying 
- Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general: Areas dominated by graminoid vegetation with less than 10% tree cover and less than 20% shrub cover, ranging from tropical lowlands to alpine meadows.Indian grasslands include Terai alluvial grasslands with tall grasses (Saccharum, Phragmites) reaching 3-5m height, semi-arid grasslands of the Deccan dominated by Sehima-Dichanthium communities, alpine meadows above treeline with Danthonia, Festuca, and cushion plants, and seasonal grasslands in forest clearings. These ecosystems show strong seasonal patterns tied to monsoon cycles, with peak biomass in the post-monsoon period and senescence during dry months, except alpine meadows showing summer growth patterns. Grass height, density, and species composition vary with moisture gradients, soil types, grazing pressure, and fire regimes.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB (432), grasslands appear light green to golden-brown depending on season.
- In NIR-R-G (543), they show moderate red during the growing season, fading to brown in dry periods
- in SWIR-NIR-R (654), they show beige-pink colors. 
- Seasonal NDVI variations are pronounced (0.2-0.6), with rapid greening after monsoon onset and gradual senescence through the dry season
- Burnt areas show distinctive black signatures temporarily
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Smooth
- Shape: Irregular
- Pattern: Shattered

Description Ecological - general: Areas where water is at, near, or above the land surface for sufficient time to support hydrophytic vegetation, including marshes, swamps, and seasonally flooded grasslands. Wetlands comprise permanent marshes with emergent vegetation (Typha, Cyperus), seasonal floodplains with flood-adapted grasses and sedges, freshwater swamps with hydrophytic shrubs and trees, and floating/submerged aquatic vegetation in shallow water bodies. These systems show strong hydroperiod influences, with vegetation composition and structure varying from permanently inundated areas with floating plants to seasonally flooded zones with flood-tolerant terrestrial species. Regional examples include Kashmir wetlands with Phragmites reed beds, Loktak's floating phumdis in Manipur, and extensive Keoladeo-type seasonal wetlands in the Gangetic plains.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB (432), wetlands appear dark green to blue-green with water showing through vegetation
- In NIR-R-G (543), they show variable red tones depending on vegetation density, with open water appearing black
- In SWIR-NIR-R (654), wetlands display bright greenish tones. 
- Seasonal variations are dramatic, with monsoon/post-monsoon showing extensive water and lush vegetation signatures, whilst the dry season may show exposed soil or dried vegetation. This temporal variability is key for wetland identification and classification. This should also show in the NDVI plots.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Medium to coarse
- Shape: Varrying
- Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general: Areas dominated by woody vegetation less than 5m height with multi-stemmed shrubs covering more than 20% but tree cover less than 10%. Scrublands include thorny scrub of arid zones dominated by Prosopis, Acacia, Ziziphus species, degraded forest areas with Lantana and other invasive shrubs, high altitude alpine scrub with Rhododendron, Juniperus above treeline, and coastal scrub on sandy/rocky substrates. These formations typically show drought adaptations, including thorns, reduced leaves, and deep root systems in arid zones, whilst montane scrubs show cushion growth forms and seasonal deciduousness. Scrublands often represent either climax vegetation in moisture-limited or temperature-limited environments, or degradation stages of former forests.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB (4-3-2), scrubs appear grey-green to brown with sparse texture visible.
- In NIR-R-G (5-4-3), they show dull red to pink tones indicating lower biomass than forests.
- in SWIR-NIR-R (6-5-4), they display bright tones due to exposed soil between shrubs. 
- Seasonal variations depend on scrub type: arid scrubs green briefly after rains, then remain brown, alpine scrubs show summer growth, whilst degraded scrubs may maintain irregular green patches year-round where invasive evergreen species dominate.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Coarse
- Shape: Varrying
- Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general:
Areas where exposed rock surfaces dominate with sparse vegetation (<20% cover) restricted to crevices, ledges, and pockets of accumulated soil.
Rocky outcrops include granite inselbergs of peninsular India with specialised lithophytic communities, limestone karst with unique calcicole flora, high-altitude rocky slopes with cushion plants and crevice-dwelling species, and lateritic plateaus with ephemeral monsoon flora. Vegetation comprises drought-adapted succulents, resurrection plants, endemic herbs appearing during monsoon, and scattered stunted trees in soil pockets. These areas support high endemism due to isolation and extreme conditions, with vegetation showing extreme seasonal variation from bare rock to brief flowering displays.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB (432), rocky outcrops appear grey to reddish-brown with scattered green patches.
- In NIR-R-G (543), they show predominantly grey/white rock with (small) red spots of vegetation;
- in SWIR-NIR-R, bright white to yellow/bright green signatures dominate due to high rock reflectance. 
- During the monsoon, temporary greening occurs in crevices and shallow soils, creating a speckled pattern, whilst dry season shows nearly bare rock signatures
- The high contrast between rock and vegetation aids in identification.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
Texture: Medium/Rough
Shape: Shape of the rock can be distinguished but irregular shapes
Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general: Heterogeneous open natural areas not fitting other herbaceous/shrub categories, including badlands, ravines, and mixed open vegetation mosaics. This category encompasses ravine systems like the Chambal badlands with sparse xerophytic vegetation on eroded slopes, degraded grasslands with irregular shrub invasion, rocky areas with grass-shrub mosaics not qualifying as pure rocky outcrops or scrublands, and disturbed natural areas in early succession. These areas typically show high spatial heterogeneity with bare soil, grass patches, scattered shrubs, and erosion features creating complex patterns. Vegetation cover varies from 20-60% with no single life form dominating, often representing transitional or degraded states between defined vegetation types.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB (432), these areas show mottled brown, grey, and pale green patterns. 
- In NIR-R-G (543), they display heterogeneous signatures with pink to grey patches reflecting varied vegetation cover.
- in SWIR-NIR-R, bright soil signatures mix with darker vegetation patches, creating high textural variance. 
- Seasonal changes are irregular and patch-specific, with some areas greening after rains whilst others remain bare
- Erosion features like gullies appear as linear dark features, helping distinguish ravine systems from other mixed vegetation.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
Texture: Medium/Rough
Shape: Irregular to some extent linear for ravines
Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general:
Agricultural lands under cultivation with herbaceous crops completing their life cycle within one year, including single and multiple cropping systems.
 This includes kharif crops (eg, rice, cotton, maize) grown during monsoon, rabi crops (eg, wheat, mustard, gram) in winter, and zaid crops (eg, watermelon, cucumber) in summer, with cropping intensity varying from single-cropped rainfed areas to triple-cropped irrigated zones. Field patterns range from small, fragmented holdings (<1 ha) in intensively cultivated plains to larger mechanised farms in Punjab-Haryana, with irrigation infrastructure (canals, tubewells) enabling multiple cropping. The agricultural calendar varies regionally: rice-wheat systems dominate the Indo-Gangetic plains, cotton-groundnut in Gujarat, rice-rice in coastal areas, and millet-pulse systems in dryland regions.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, crops vary from bare soil (brown) during ploughing to bright green at peak growth to golden during harvest 
- In NIR-R-G they show dramatic temporal changes from black (water in rice fields) to brilliant red (peak vegetation) to brown (harvest)
- In SWIR-NIR-R signatures cycle from blue (planted/flooded fields) through red (growing crop) to bright yellow (mature crop). 
- Multi-temporal imagery reveals cropping patterns with 2-3 distinct growth cycles annually in irrigated areas versus a single peak in rainfed regions - please see NDVI plots
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Smooth
- Shape: Regular shape (fields)
- Pattern: regular - field boundaries and irrigation channels create characteristic geometric patterns distinguishing agriculture from natural vegetation.

Description Ecological - general:
Agricultural lands with perennial woody crops, including tree plantations, orchards, and shrub crops, maintaining permanent cover for multiple years.
This encompasses tea gardens on Himalayan and Western Ghats slopes with manicured shrubs and shade trees, coffee plantations under forest canopy or as monocultures, rubber plantations with regular spacing and seasonal latex tapping, fruit orchards (mango, citrus, apple) with seasonal flowering and fruiting cycles, and coconut/arecanut gardens often with multi-tier cropping. These systems show distinct management signatures, including regular spacing, pruning patterns, shade trees in tea/coffee, and intercropping in coconut gardens. Regional specialisations include rubber in Kerala and North-East, tea in Assam and Nilgiris, coffee in Karnataka and Kerala, apples in Himachal Pradesh, and citrus in North-East and central India.
Description FCC - general:
In RGB (4-3-2), perennial crops appear consistently green with regular textural patterns from planted rows
- in NIR-R-G (5-4-3), they show steady red signatures with geometric patterns visible, varying in intensity with management practices
- In SWIR-NIR-R (6-5-4), they display moderate bright green year-round with subtle seasonal variations. 
- Unlike natural forests, these areas show regular spacing patterns, access roads, and processing infrastructure.
- Seasonal variations are subtle except for deciduous fruit orchards showing winter leaf fall, whilst tea gardens show periodic brightness changes after pruning cycles.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
Texture: Medium to coarse
Shape: Regular
Pattern: can be quite regular (orchards, planted rows, e.g), visible geometric patterns, access roads and and processing infrastructure.

Description Ecological - general:
Planted stands of native or exotic tree species established primarily for timber production, pulpwood, or restoration purposes.
 Forest plantations include teak and eucalyptus monocultures for timber and pulpwood, pine plantations in hills for resin and timber, bamboo plantations for the paper industry, abandoned plantations undergoing naturalisation with native species recruitment, and mixed species restoration plantings. These display characteristic even-aged stands with uniform height, regular spacing creating visible row patterns, minimal understory in active plantations, and varying management intensity from regularly thinned stands to abandoned areas. Rotation periods vary from 5-7 years for eucalyptus and bamboo to 30-60 years for teak, with clear-felling creating distinctive landscape patterns.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, plantations show uniform green with geometric patterns visible at high resolution,
in NIR-R-G, they display consistent bright red in rows or blocks, contrasting with irregular natural forest
- In SWIR-NIR-R, they show homogeneous green tones for active plantations, more variable for abandoned ones. 
- Temporal signatures reveal management activities: clear-cut areas appear as sudden brown patches, young plantations show increasing vigour over the years, whilst abandoned plantations gradually develop heterogeneous signatures as natural species establish.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
Texture: Medium / relatively smooth in comparison to a natural forest where the canopy structure is more uneven. More coarse if the trees are more mature. 
Shape: Regular. rectangular, square, or straight-edged because plantations can typically show lines according plantations. 
Pattern: Regular (plantations can show up  as a regular pattern pattern spatially, geometric patterns at high resolution (or zooming in) present. Plantations across lines with even spacing, parallel lines, clusters with identical patterns

Description Ecological - general: Agricultural landscapes with intimate mixtures of different crop types, field sizes, and agricultural practices that cannot be separated at mapping resolution.  This includes smallholder farming systems with mixed cropping and crop rotations within small fields, agroforestry mosaics combining trees with crops in complex patterns (like homegardens), peri-urban agricultural areas with vegetables, flowers, and nurseries interspersed with built-up areas, and shifting cultivation patches in various fallow stages. These areas characterise much of India's agricultural landscape, where field sizes are below mapping resolution, farmers practice diverse cropping systems, and agricultural lands intermix with trees, settlements, and other land uses. Regional examples include Kerala homegardens, North-Eastern jhum cultivation mosaics, and peri-urban farming around major cities.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, mosaics show a patchwork of greens, browns, and intermediate tones without clear patterns
 - In NIR-R-G, they display heterogeneous red signatures with high spatial variance at the pixel level
- In SWIR-NIR-R, they show mixed signatures, preventing clear crop type identification. Temporal patterns are complex, with different patches showing asynchronous planting and harvesting, making single-date classification difficult; multi-temporal analysis reveals the agricultural nature through seasonal changes, though specific crop identification remains challenging without sub-pixel analysis techniques.-
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Rough
- Shape: Irregular
- Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general:
Areas dominated by constructed materials, including buildings, roads, and other impervious surfaces associated with human settlements and infrastructure.
Built-up areas encompass dense urban cores with multi-storey buildings and complete impervious cover, suburban areas mixing buildings with gardens and open spaces, rural settlements with clustered or dispersed houses amid agricultural lands, and linear infrastructure including highways, railways, and canal networks. Indian cities show characteristic dense organic growth patterns in old cores, planned colonies with geometric layouts, informal settlements with high density and irregular patterns, and expanding peri-urban zones where agricultural lands are progressively converted. Industrial areas, airports, and institutional campuses create distinct large-footprint features with specific spectral signatures.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB (432), built-up areas appear grey to white for concrete, blue-grey for metal roofs, and red-brown for traditional tile/clay roofs
- In NIR-R-G, they show cyan to blue-grey due to low vegetation, with parks appearing as red patches
- in SWIR-NIR-R, they display bright white to yellow signatures from high reflectance of impervious surfaces. 
- Urban areas show stable signatures year-round, unlike agricultural areas, though urban vegetation shows seasonal variations
- Thermal imagery reveals urban heat islands, whilst night-time lights effectively delineate settlement extents and infrastructure networks.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Coarse
- Shape: Regular (city blocks)
- Pattern: Regular/geometric

Description Ecological - general: Unconsolidated sediment zones between the mean low tide and the permanent vegetation line or cliff base along coastlines.Beaches comprise sandy shores along India's 7,500km coastline, varying from wide sandy expanses (Marina Beach, Puri) to narrow strips below cliffs, including composition variations from white coral sand to black mineral sand beaches. They display dynamic morphology with seasonal and storm-driven changes in width and profile, wrack lines marking high tide limits with debris accumulation, and varying levels of human modification from pristine to heavily developed tourist beaches. Beaches grade landward into dunes or directly into vegetation, whilst seaward they extend to surf zones, with width varying from metres to hundreds of metres based on tidal range and coastal geomorphology.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, beaches appear white to light yellow for dry sand, darker when wet.
 - in NIR-R-G, they show white to light grey with sharp contrast against dark water;.
- In SWIR-NIR-R, they display brilliant white signatures distinguishing them from all other land covers. 
- Tidal stage during image acquisition significantly affects beach width and spectral properties, with wet sand showing darker signatures.
- Seasonal variations include width changes during monsoons and spectral changes from moisture, whilst human activities create distinct patterns like beach shacks and access roads.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
Texture: Homogenous/smooth but more coarse in case the beach has pebbles
Shape: Light strips around water, clear boundary between sea and water.
Pattern: Gradual change from sea to sand, ripple marks if you zoom in

Description Ecological - general:
Aeolian landforms composed of wind-deposited sand, occurring in coastal and inland desert environments with sufficient sand supply and wind energy.
Sand dunes include coastal dune systems along western and eastern coasts with vegetation-stabilised foredunes and mobile parabolic dunes, extensive inland dune fields in Rajasthan's Thar Desert with barchan, longitudinal, and transverse forms, and riverine point-bar dunes along major rivers during the dry season. Active dunes show mobile crests and slip faces with sparse or no vegetation, whilst stable/semi-stable dunes support xerophytic grasses (Saccharum) and shrubs (Calotropis, Prosopis), with dune morphology and movement rates controlled by wind regime, sand supply, and vegetation cover. Coastal dunes often show zonation from mobile foredunes through stable backdunes to scrub vegetation.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, dunes appear bright white to yellow for bare sand, with darker patches where vegetation establishes. 
- In NIR-R-G, they show pinkish colors
- In SWIR-NIR-R, bright white signatures dominate with exceptional reflectance in SWIR bands. 
- Dune crests and slip faces create characteristic shadow patterns aiding morphology interpretation; seasonal variations include slight darkening during monsoons from moisture and temporary vegetation on semi-stable dunes, whilst dune migration can be tracked through multi-temporal imagery showing systematic positional changes.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture:  Fine (sand)/homogenous
- Shape: Irregular (long, crescent, Ushape)
- Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general:
Areas where earth materials are extracted through surface or near-surface excavation, including active mines, quarries, and associated waste deposits.
Mining areas encompass open-cast coal mines in Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Jharkhand with vast excavations and overburden dumps, iron ore mines in Karnataka, Goa, and Odisha showing red-brown excavations, limestone quarries for the cement industry appearing as white scars, sand mining along rivers creating pits and stockpiles, and stone quarries on hillsides with benched excavations. These areas display characteristic disturbed topography with excavation pits, overburden/waste dumps, haul roads, processing infrastructure, and settling ponds, often with a complete absence of vegetation in active areas. Abandoned mines may show varying degrees of natural colonisation or engineered restoration with plantations.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, mining areas show varied colours from white (limestone) to red (iron ore) to black (coal) depending on extracted material
- In NIR-R-G, they appear in stark non-vegetated tones contrasting sharply with surroundings
- In SWIR-NIR-R, they display very bright signatures due to exposed mineral surfaces and absence of moisture. 
- Temporal analysis reveals expanding excavations, growing waste dumps, and new access roads; water-filled abandoned pits appear black in NIR, whilst rehabilitation efforts show gradually increasing vegetation signatures over time.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Irregular
- Shape: Irregular pits or benches for open pit mines
- Pattern: irregular / Distinguish roads around pits, terrace stepped

Description Ecological - general: Exposed soil or rock surfaces lacking vegetation due to natural or anthropogenic factors, not classified under specific non-vegetated categories. This includes naturally bare areas like erosion-exposed soils on steep slopes and landslide scars, barren lands with soil limitations (salinity, alkalinity) preventing vegetation establishment, temporarily bare areas including harvested fields and construction sites, degraded lands with severe erosion exposing subsoil or bedrock, and mudflats in coastal and inland water bodies during low water periods. These areas often represent transitional states between vegetated and permanently non-vegetated categories, with potential for vegetation establishment given changed conditions or management. The distinction from rocky outcrops (2.4) is the absence of specialised lithophytic vegetation and the often temporary nature of bareness.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, bare areas show colours reflecting soil mineralogy from red (iron-rich) to white (salt) to grey (alluvial);
- In NIR-R-G, they appear brown to grey with no red vegetation signal
- in SWIR-NIR-R, they show bright signatures varying with soil moisture and composition. 
- Seasonal variations depend on the  cause of bareness: agricultural areas show cyclic vegetation-bare patterns, erosion areas may green slightly during monsoons, whilst salt-affected areas remain consistently bare; soil moisture after rain events temporarily darkens spectral signatures across all bands.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
Texture: Fine texture
Shape: Can be as as well regular or irregular
Pattern: Smooth

Description Ecological - general: Natural flowing watercourses, including perennial and seasonal streams, from mountain torrents to meandering alluvial channels. Rivers range from Himalayan snow-fed perennial systems (Ganga, Brahmaputra) with high discharge and sediment loads, to peninsular seasonal rivers dependent on monsoon rainfall, including braided channels with multiple threads and mid-channel bars in alluvial reaches, and incised channels in rocky terrain. They display seasonal flow variations from flooding during monsoons to reduced flow or dry beds in summer, with water quality varying from clear mountain streams to sediment-laden plains rivers, affecting spectral properties. Channel morphology includes straight, meandering, braided, and anastomosing patterns, with associated features like oxbow lakes, point bars, and riparian zones.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, rivers appear blue to brown depending on sediment load.
- In NIR-R-G, they show black to dark blue due to complete NIR absorption by water.
- In SWIR-NIR-R, they appear black as water absorbs strongly in both NIR and SWIR bands
- Seasonal variations are dramatic: monsoon flooding expands water extent beyond normal channels
- Dry season reveals sand bars and reduced flow, whilst sediment plumes during high flow create brown tones extending downstream
- Narrow streams may be obscured by riparian vegetation requiring SWIR bands for detection.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Smooth
- Shape: Irregular
- Pattern: Irregular

Description Ecological - general:
Areas covered by seasonal or permanent snow and ice, including glaciers, snowfields, and frozen water bodies.
This encompasses Himalayan glaciers from large valley glaciers (Gangotri, Siachen) to small cirque glaciers, with accumulation zones above snowline and ablation zones below, seasonal snow cover varying with elevation and aspect, typically above 3000m in winter extending to 5000m+ in summer, and frozen lakes and rivers at high elevations during winter months. Snow and ice features show distinct zonation from fresh snow (high albedo) to firn to glacier ice (lower albedo), with glacier surfaces featuring crevasses, icefalls, and debris cover in ablation zones. Climate change impacts are evident through retreating glacier termini, expanding proglacial lakes, and reduced snow cover duration.
Description FCC - general:
- RGB (432) - Snow and glaciers appear white
- NIR-SWIR-R - Snow and glaciers seem purple
- SWIR-NIR-R, snow appears uniquely cyan to blue due to ice absorption in SWIR whilst maintaining NIR reflectance
- Seasonal patterns show maximum snow extent in winter (January-February) and minimum in late summer (August-September)
glacier flow creates distinctive patterns, whilst avalanche deposits and seasonal snow can be distinguished from permanent ice through multi-temporal analysis.
Description: Texture, shape and pattern:
- Texture: Smooth (fresh snow), fine grained (e.g. wind), coarse (melting snow),. For glaciers: More streaked and showing crevisses.
- Shape: Snow not very much a shape
glaciers - fllow lines and crevasses for glaciers
Pattern: Flow lines and crevasses in glaciers in comparison to snow

Description Ecological - general:
Flat expanses where saline water evaporates, leaving salt deposits, including natural playas and artificial evaporation ponds.
Salt pans include extensive artificial seawater evaporation ponds along Gujarat and Tamil Nadu coasts for salt production, natural inland salt lakes like Sambhar in Rajasthan with seasonal water and salt crust cycles, and small seasonal pans in arid regions filling during monsoons then evaporating to leave salt deposits. These features show characteristic sequences from brine ponds (varying salinity affecting colour) to crystalliser ponds to harvest-ready salt beds, with associated infrastructure including bunds, channels, and salt mounds in commercial operations. Natural salt pans display seasonal cycles of flooding, evaporation, and salt crystallisation, supporting specialised halophytic vegetation on margins.
Description FCC - general:
- In RGB, salt pans vary from white (dry salt) to pink/green (brine with algae) to blue (water-filled)
- The characteristics look quite different in general whether the salt pans are for salt production or
are natural salt pans. 
-  In NIR-R-G, they show white for salt crusts, black for brine, with marginal vegetation appearing red
-  In SWIR-NIR-R, dry salt appears brilliant white whilst brine shows varying absorption based on depth and salinity.
- Seasonal patterns in natural pans show flooding during monsoons (dark/blue signatures) transitioning through evaporation stages to white salt crusts in the dry season
-  commercial salt pans show systematic colour gradients across evaporation sequences, with harvest cycles visible as patches of scraped versus unharvested areas.
